ur.d: Cidade suméria no sul da Mesopotâmia, ponto de partida de Abrão com Terá. A identificação com Tell el-Muqayyar é a mais aceita; alguns propõem um local no norte (hipótese).

hara.d: Cidade comercial no alto Eufrates onde Terá morreu e Abrão recebeu a ordem de partir para Canaã.

siquem.d: Primeira parada de Abrão em Canaã, onde Deus prometeu a terra. Mais tarde, local da renovação da aliança com Josué.

betel.d: Abrão levantou um altar entre Betel e Ai; Jacó teve ali o sonho da escada.

ai.d: Cidade conquistada por Josué após a derrota inicial. A localização exata é debatida pelos arqueólogos.

hebrom.d: Onde Abraão habitou junto aos carvalhos de Manre e comprou a caverna de Macpela. Primeira capital de Davi.

gerar.d: Região filisteia onde Abraão e depois Isaque peregrinaram.

berseba.d: Poço da aliança entre Abraão e Abimeleque; limite sul de Israel (“de Dã a Berseba”).

moria.d: Abraão foi chamado a oferecer Isaque num dos montes de Moriá; 2 Crônicas identifica Moriá com o monte do templo.

egito.d: Abrão desceu ao Egito na fome; José foi governador ali; Israel viveu no Egito até o êxodo.

ramesses.d: Cidade-armazém no delta oriental, ponto de partida do êxodo.

marvermelho.d: O texto chama o mar de yam suph (“mar de juncos”/Mar Vermelho). Há várias propostas: lagos Amargos, golfo de Suez ou golfo de Ácaba. O ponto no mapa é ilustrativo.

sinai.d: Onde Deus deu a Lei a Moisés. A identificação com Jebel Musa remonta a uma tradição cristã do séc. IV; outras propostas incluem montes no norte do Sinai e na Arábia.

cades.d: Base de Israel no deserto; de lá saíram os doze espias. Israel vagou quase 38 anos até deixar a região.

nebo.d: De onde Moisés viu a terra prometida e onde morreu.

sitim.d: Último acampamento de Israel antes de atravessar o Jordão.

gilgal.d: Primeiro acampamento em Canaã, com as doze pedras do Jordão.

jerico.d: Uma das cidades mais antigas do mundo; muralhas caíram diante de Israel.

gibeom.d: Os gibeonitas fizeram aliança com Josué; batalha em que o sol se deteve.

laquis.d: Cidade fortificada de Judá; tomada por Josué e, séculos depois, cercada pelos assírios (701 a.C.).

hazor.d: “Cabeça de todos aqueles reinos” no norte; queimada por Josué.

silo.d: Onde o tabernáculo ficou nos dias dos juízes; ali Ana orou e Samuel serviu.

da.d: Cidade no extremo norte de Israel; Jeroboão pôs ali um bezerro de ouro.

samaria.d: Capital do Reino do Norte, fundada por Onri; caiu diante da Assíria em 722 a.C.

jerusalem.d: Cidade de Davi e do templo; centro da história bíblica, da morte e ressurreição de Jesus e do início da igreja.

ninive.d: Capital do Império Assírio; Jonas pregou ali. Destruída em 612 a.C.

babilonia.d: Capital do império de Nabucodonosor; para lá Judá foi levado em cativeiro.

susa.d: Capital persa onde se passam Ester e o início de Neemias.

damasco.d: Capital dos arameus; na estrada de Damasco Saulo encontrou o Cristo ressuscitado.

tiro.d: Grande porto fenício; Hirão forneceu cedro para o templo. Paulo passou ali na terceira viagem.

sidom.d: Cidade fenícia; parada de Paulo a caminho de Roma.

gaza.d: Cidade filisteia; caminho de Jerusalém a Gaza foi onde Filipe encontrou o eunuco etíope.

megido.d: Fortaleza estratégica no vale de Jezreel.

jope.d: Porto onde Jonas embarcou e onde Pedro ressuscitou Tabita e teve a visão do lençol.

belem.d: Cidade de Davi; nascimento de Jesus.

betabara.d: Onde João batizava e Jesus foi batizado (local exato debatido).

cana.d: Primeiro sinal de Jesus: a água transformada em vinho.

cafarnaum.d: Centro do ministério de Jesus na Galileia; casa de Pedro.

betsaida.d: Cidade de Pedro, André e Filipe.

cesfilipe.d: Onde Pedro confessou: “Tu és o Cristo”.

sicar.d: Conversa de Jesus com a mulher samaritana.

betania.d: Casa de Marta, Maria e Lázaro; local da ressurreição de Lázaro.

emaus.d: O Ressuscitado caminhou com dois discípulos.

cesareia.d: Capital romana da Judeia; conversão de Cornélio; Paulo ficou preso ali dois anos.

azoto.d: Onde Filipe reapareceu depois do batismo do eunuco.

antioquia.d: Ali os discípulos foram chamados cristãos pela primeira vez; base das viagens missionárias de Paulo.

seleucia.d: Porto de Antioquia, de onde partiu a primeira viagem.

salamina.d: Paulo e Barnabé pregaram nas sinagogas.

pafos.d: Conversão do procônsul Sérgio Paulo; Elimas ficou cego.

perge.d: João Marcos voltou a Jerusalém daqui.

atalia.d: Porto de onde Paulo e Barnabé voltaram a Antioquia.

antpisidia.d: Grande sermão de Paulo na sinagoga.

iconio.d: Muitos creram; perseguição obrigou a fuga.

listra.d: Cura de um coxo; Paulo apedrejado; cidade de Timóteo.

derbe.d: Muitos discípulos; ponto final da primeira viagem antes do retorno.

troade.d: Visão do varão macedônio; ressurreição de Êutico.

samotracia.d: Escala marítima a caminho da Macedônia.

neapolis.d: Porto de Filipos; primeiro desembarque de Paulo na Europa.

filipos.d: Conversão de Lídia e do carcereiro; Paulo e Silas presos e libertos.

tessalonica.d: Igreja formada em poucas semanas; tumulto contra Jasom.

bereia.d: Os bereanos examinavam as Escrituras todos os dias.

corinto.d: Paulo ficou um ano e meio; Áquila e Priscila; inscrição de Gálio confirma a data (c. 51–52 d.C.).

cencreia.d: Porto oriental de Corinto; igreja de Febe.

efeso.d: Paulo ensinou ali cerca de três anos; tumulto dos ourives; igreja de Apocalipse 2.

mileto.d: Despedida de Paulo aos presbíteros de Éfeso.

patara.d: Troca de navio rumo à Fenícia.

ptolemaida.d: Paulo saudou os irmãos por um dia.

mirra.d: Paulo foi transferido para um navio de Alexandria.

cnido.d: Ventos contrários na viagem a Roma.

bonsportos.d: Paulo aconselhou passar o inverno ali.

malta.d: Naufrágio; Paulo picado por uma víbora; cura do pai de Públio.

puteoli.d: Paulo encontrou irmãos e ficou sete dias.

forum.n: Fórum de Ápio e Três Vendas
forum.d: Irmãos de Roma vieram ao encontro de Paulo.

roma.d: Capital do império; Paulo ficou dois anos em casa alugada pregando o Reino. Segundo a tradição, Pedro e Paulo morreram ali sob Nero.

tiatira.d: Igreja de Apocalipse 2; cidade de Lídia.

laodiceia.d: Igreja de Apocalipse 3; ligada a Colossos.

colossos.d: Igreja que recebeu a carta aos Colossenses.

alexandria.d: Grande centro judaico e cristão; cidade de Apolo.

patras.d: Segundo uma tradição tardia, local do martírio do apóstolo André.

arabia.d: Paulo foi para a Arábia logo após a conversão; a região exata não é dita.

cirene.d: Cidade de Simão, que carregou a cruz.

jornadas.resumo: From Ur of the Chaldeans to Canaan: the pilgrimage of Abraham's faith, with the promise of land and descendants.
jornadas.nota: The cities are mentioned in the text; the paths between them are approximate.

etapas.t: He will have died; called God
Promise of the earth and altar

jornadas.data: c. 1446 a.C. (datação antiga, 1Rs 6:1) ou c. 1260 a.C. (datação tardia)
jornadas.resumo: The departure from Egypt, the crossing of the sea, the Law at Sinai, and forty years in the desert up to the plains of Moab.
jornadas.nota: The route of the Exodus is one of the most debated questions in biblical geography. The intermediate points and the route are reconstructions; only the general direction is safe.

etapas.nota: Debated location; illustrative point
Uncertain location
Uncertain location
Traditional location (Jebel Musa); other hypotheses

etapas.t: Moses sees the earth and dies
etapas.nota: Approximate route through the east (Edom and Moab)

jornadas.data: c. 1406–1400 a.C. (datação antiga) ou séc. XIII a.C. (datação tardia)
jornadas.resumo: The crossing of the Jordan and Joshua's campaigns in the center, south, and north of Canaan.

etapas.t: Renewal of the covenant (Ebal and Gerizim)
Alliance with Gibeon; the sun stands still
The tabernacle in Shiloh; division of the land

jornadas.resumo: The Northern Kingdom was taken by Assyria; Judah, by Babylon, as the prophets had foretold.

etapas.nota: Confirmed in the annals of Sargon II (H)
Destinations: Hala, Habor, and the cities of the Medes
Babylonian chronicles confirm 597 BC (H)
Route through the Fertile Crescent, not through the desert

jornadas.resumo: With Cyrus's decree, the exiles returned, rebuilt the temple and then the walls of Jerusalem.

etapas.nota: The Cylinder of Cyrus (H) shows the Persian policy of returning peoples
Route through the north, skirting the desert

jornadas.resumo: From birth in Bethlehem to the cross and resurrection in Jerusalem: the main places of Jesus' ministry.
jornadas.nota: The order of events in Galilee is simplified; the Gospels do not provide a complete itinerary.

etapas.nota: Exact location debated
Uncertain location

jornadas.resumo: From persecutor to apostle: the road to Damascus, Arabia, Tarsus, and Antioch.

etapas.nota: Exact region not provided

etapas.t: Return to Damascus; escape through the wall

jornadas.resumo: Sent by the church of Antioch, Paul and Barnabas bring the gospel to Cyprus and southern Galatia.
With Silas and then Timothy, Paul crosses into Europe: Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Athens, and Corinth.

etapas.nota: Tarsus is not mentioned; probable passage
Route through the region, approximate

etapas.t: A year and a half; letters to the Thessalonians
etapas.nota: Date confirmed by the inscription of Gálio (H)
The ascent to Jerusalem implied in the text

jornadas.resumo: Almost three years in Ephesus, visits to the churches of Macedonia and Greece, and the final journey to Jerusalem.

etapas.nota: Approximate route

etapas.t: Three months in Greece; letter to the Romans
etapas.nota: Corinth is probable, not cited (Hp)

etapas.t: House of Philip; prophecy of Agabus

jornadas.resumo: Imprisoned, Paul appeals to Caesar and travels to Rome: storm, shipwreck in Malta, and arrival at the empire's capital.

etapas.nota: The exact drift route is approximate

etapas.t: Forum of Appius and Three Sales

jornadas.resumo: From the Sea of Galilee to Rome: the fisherman called to be a fisherman of men.
jornadas.nota: Acts stops narrating Peter's life after chapter 15.

etapas.nota: The presence and death of Peter in Rome under Nero are attested by Clement of Rome, Ignatius, Irenaeus, and Eusebius (T). "Babylon" in 1 Pet 5:13 is often read as Rome (Hp). The upside-down crucifixion comes from later writings (T).

jornadas.resumo: One of the seven deacons, he brought the gospel to Samaria and the Ethiopian eunuch and settled in Caesarea.
jornadas.nota: Not to be confused with the apostle Philip, one of the Twelve.

etapas.t: Married in Caesarea; four prophetess daughters

jornadas.resumo: The beloved disciple: from Galilee to Jerusalem, Samaria, Patmos, and, according to tradition, Ephesus.

etapas.t: At the foot of the cross; witness of the resurrection

etapas.nota: Irenaeus (2nd century) states that John lived in Ephesus until the time of Trajan (T).
Ancient tradition; there is no biblical account.

mapas.resumo: The division of land among the tribes. The names are in the approximate region of each inheritance; the exact boundaries are described in Joshua, but several are debated.
mapas.nota: Undrawn borders: awaiting detailed cartographic research.

mapas.nome: The kingdoms of Israel and Judah
mapas.resumo: After Solomon (c. 930 BC), the kingdom was divided: Israel to the north, with its capital in Samaria, and Judah to the south, with its capital in Jerusalem.
Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, and Persia successively dominated the Near East and shaped the history of Israel.

mapas.nome: The seven churches of the Apocalypse
mapas.resumo: The seven churches of Asia that received Christ's letters in Revelation 2 and 3, and the island of Patmos.

mapas.nome: The expansion of the church in Acts
mapas.resumo: "You will be my witnesses both in Jerusalem and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth" (Acts 1:8).

perfis.resumo: Pharisee of Tarsus, persecutor of the church, called by the risen Christ to bring the gospel to the nations.

itens.x: Born in Tarsus, Roman citizen, educated in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel.
He persecuted the church; he consented to Stephen's death.
Meeting with Christ on the road to Damascus and baptism by Ananias.
Arabia, Damascus, Jerusalem, Tarsus, and Antioch in the early years.
Three missionary journeys through Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia, and Asia.
Almost three years in Ephesus.
Companions: Barnabas, John Mark, Silas, Timothy, Luke, Titus, Aquila, and Priscilla.
Churches planted or strengthened in Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe, Philippi, Thessalonica, Berea, Corinth, and Ephesus.
Sermons in Antioch of Pisidia, Lystra, in the Areopagus, and in Miletus.
Thirteen letters from the New Testament bear his name.
The date of his stay in Corinth is confirmed by Gallus's inscription at Delphi (c. 51–52 AD).
Imprisoned in Jerusalem, two years in Caesarea, appeal to Caesar and journey to Rome.
Two years under house arrest in Rome, preaching the Kingdom.
New arrest and expectation of death in 2 Timothy.
Possible trip to Spain: Paul planned it (Rom 15:24); Clement of Rome says he reached "the edge of the West" — a debated interpretation.
Martyrdom in Rome under Nero, by beheading, c. 64–67 AD.

perfis.resumo: Fisherman from Galilee, called by Jesus, spokesman of the Twelve and one of the pillars of the church in Jerusalem.

itens.x: Native of Bethsaida; lived in Capernaum; brought to Jesus by Andrew.
Called by the sea: "fishermen of men."
Confession in Caesarea Philippi; denial and restoration.
Leadership in Jerusalem after Pentecost.
With John in Samaria; Lyda, Joppa, and Caesarea (Cornelius).
Antioch, where he was confronted by Paul.
Pentecost Sermon; speech at the Council of Jerusalem.
Two letters bear his name.
Jesus indicated the manner of his death.
Presence and martyrdom in Rome under Nero (c. 64–68 AD).
Crucified upside down — account of later writings.

perfis.resumo: Fisherman, brother of James, called "son of thunder" and identified by tradition as the beloved disciple.

itens.x: Called with Tiago while fixing the nets.
Present at the Transfiguration, in Gethsemane, and at the foot of the cross.
Column of the church of Jerusalem, with Peter and James.
With Peter in the temple and in Samaria.
The Gospel of John, the three letters, and the Apocalypse are traditionally attributed to him.
He received the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos.
He lived in Ephesus until old age and died a natural death.

perfis.resumo: Brother of John, from Jesus' closest circle and the first of the Twelve to die for Christ.

itens.x: Called with his brother João.
Present at the Transfiguration and in Gethsemane.
Killed by the sword by Herod Agrippa I in Jerusalem, c. 44 AD.
Traditions about preaching in Spain arise centuries later and have no ancient support.

perfis.resumo: Brother of Peter, disciple of John the Baptist, he was the one who brought Simon to Jesus.

itens.x: Disciple of John the Baptist; followed Jesus and called his brother.
He presented the boy with the loaves and the Greeks to Jesus.
Preaching in Scythia (Black Sea region), according to Origen cited by Eusebius.
Martyrdom in Patras, in Achaea; the X-shaped cross is a medieval tradition.

perfis.resumo: A native of Bethsaida, Nathanael called Jesus.

itens.x: Called by Jesus in Galilee; he took Nathanael.
"Lord, show us the Father."
Death in Hierapolis, Asia, according to Polycrates of Ephesus.
Ancient sources sometimes confuse him with Philip the evangelist.

perfis.resumo: Known for doubt and for the confession "My Lord and my God."

itens.x: "Let us also go to die with him."
Confession before the Risen One.
Preaching in Parthia, according to Origen.
Mission and martyrdom in India (Mylapore), tradition recorded in the Acts of Thomas (3rd century) and preserved by the Christians of Saint Thomas. Outside the area of this map.

perfis.resumo: Tax collector in Capernaum called by Jesus.

itens.x: Called at the collection office.
The first Gospel is attributed to him since Papias (2nd century). 2nd).
Traditions about the place of his death differ (Ethiopia, Parthia, Persia); there is no certainty.

perfis.resumo: Levite of Cyprus, "son of consolation," who introduced Paul to the apostles and accompanied him on the first journey.

itens.x: A native of Cyprus; he sold a field and gave it to the apostles.
He brought Paul to Jerusalem; sent to Antioch.
First journey with Paul; called apostle.
He separated from Paul because of Mark and went to Cyprus.
Martyrdom in Salamis, Cyprus — late tradition.

perfis.resumo: Leader of the Jerusalem church chosen by Paul for the second trip.

itens.x: One of the leading men sent with the council's letter.
Second journey: imprisoned with Paul in Philippi; Thessalonica, Berea, and Corinth.
Co-author in the greetings of 1 and 2 Thessalonians; secretary or bearer of 1 Peter.
There is no biblical record of the end of his life.

perfis.resumo: A young man from Lystra, son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father, he became the son in Paul's faith.

itens.x: Disciple of Lystra; mother Eunice and grandmother Loide.
Second and third voyages; sent to Thessalonica, Corinth, and Philippi.
Co-author in the greetings of several letters; recipient of 1 and 2 Timothy.
Left in Ephesus to care for the church.
He was arrested and released.
First bishop of Ephesus and martyr — tradition.

perfis.resumo: The "beloved doctor," the traditional author of the Gospels of Luke and Acts.

itens.x: He joins Paul in Troas: the passages begin in "we."
Philippi; journey to Jerusalem; journey to Rome.
Authorship of Luke and Acts: ancient and widely accepted tradition.
With Paul in Rome: "Only Luke is with me."
Death at age 84 in Boeotia — tradition uncertain.

perfis.resumo: One of the seven chosen in Acts 6; he brought the gospel to Samaria and to the Ethiopian eunuch.

itens.x: Chosen among the seven.
Samaria, Gaza road, Azotus and Caesarea.
He lived in Caesarea with four prophetic daughters when Paul passed by.
